title: Photograph: When They Listened in the "Gay Nineties"
description:
Daily Herald photograph entitled 'When They Listened in the Gay Nineties'. The photograph shows Mrs. E. A. Hiller (third from the right) and her friends gathered around a 'Listeners In' machine. The photograph, c. 1890, was printed in the Daily Herald January 28th 1958.

Photograph from the Daily Herald Archive, indexed as Music, Instruments, Gramophones, Misc.
Transcribed_Text:
MUSIC - INSTRUMENTS - GRAMAPHONES- MISC. 1983-5236/31638

WHEN THEY "LISTENED IN" IN THE "GAY NINETIES".

STRANGE TO EYES ACCUSTOMED TO THE WONDERS
OF THIS DECADE IS THIS PHOTOGRAPH FROM THE DIM,
BUT NOT SO DISTANT PAST, WHICH IS SOMETIMES KNOWN
AS THE "GAY NINETIES". THERE WERE NO RADIOS IN THOSE
DAYS BUT THERE WERE WHAT WERE CALLED "LISTENERS IN".
MRS. E. A HILLER OF SALINA, U.S.A., IS THE OWNER OF
THIS UNIQUE PHOTOGRAPH WHICH SHOWS HERSELF AND
FRIENDS OF HER CHILDHOOD ENJOYING THE RARE TREAT
AS THEY GATHERED ROUND THE MACHINE. THEY ADJUST THE
EARPIECES AND LISTEN TO THE MUSIC. THE OWNER OF THE
MACHINE IS THE ONLY MAN IN THE GROUP, LLOYD C.
MITCHELL WHO KEPT HIS MACHINE AT STREET CORNERS, OR
WHEREVER THERE WAS A CROWD OF PROSPECTIVE LISTENERS,
MRS. HILLER IS SEEN THIRD FROM RIGHT. L/B. KEYS TOPE. 12.

DAI HAD TO BRING
HIS PYJAMAS

OVER 40 years in the
mines has taken its
toll of Dai Ley, 61-year-
old president of the
Nottingham miners.
But yesterday he got
out of bed to be driven
170 miles to Llandough
Hospital, near Cardiff.
Near him stood a 150-
guinea television set
and all round were fel-
low miners. The set
was a present from
Nottingham miners to
the pneumoconiosis
centre at the hospital—
the only one of its kind
in Britain.

Dai—he was born in
Swansea—has been a
patient there three
times. He told the
Nottingham men about
it and the set was on
its way in no time.
“For,” said Dai, “the
Notts miners are grate-
ful for the agitation of
the South Wales miners
on the dust problem.”
Then he was pushed
away in a wheel chair
to have tea with the
doctors. Next came a
pair of pyjamas. Dai
was starting his fourth
term as a patient.

NOT TO BE PUBLISHED UNTIL 6 P.M. LOCAL TIME (JAMAICAN) ON THURSDAY 15TH OCTOBER 1953

VISIT OF HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN TO JAMAICA

The Governor of Jamaica (Sir Hugh Foot) has today sent the following message
to the House of Representatives and the Legislative Council of Jamaica: -

"I have been informed by the Secretary of State for the Colonies that Her
Majesty the Queen has been graciously pleased to signify her intention of
visiting Jamaica early next month. Her Majesty and the Duke of Edinburgh will
arrive in Jamaica on Wednesday the 25th November, 1953, and will leave from
Montego Bay on Friday the 27th November. In the course of their visit to Jamaica
they will attend a special meeting of the Privy Council and will be present at
military parades in Kingston and Montego Bay. Further details of the
itinerary will be published as soon as they have been decided."

The visit of the Queen to Jamaica on 25th November will mark the first
occasion on which a reigning Sovereign has ever visited this Colony and
also the first visit of Her Majesty to Jamaica since her accession.

The Governor, on behalf of the Government and people of Jamaica, has
expressed his warm and loyal satisfaction at the news of the visit and has
sent the following message to Her Majesty on behalf of the people of Jamaica:

"The people of Jamaica have heard the news of Your Majesty's visit with
feelings of profound and loyal joy. We look forward with the deepest
devotion to the arrival of Your Majesty and the Duke of Edinburgh and we
beg to offer to Your Majesty and to the Duke of Edinburgh our most humble
and sincere greetings and a most loyal and affectionate welcome to this island."

15th October, 1953.

This contract forms Phase I of a large new scheme
planned by the L.C.C. to alleviate housing problems in
London. Of the seven Blocks, Block No. 2 with 18 Storeys
Blocks (Nos. 1-4) Eight Storeys, and Blocks (Nos. 17-19) four
Storeys.

Founded on 22" Driven piling and 120 ft. Tower
Block which provides 193 dwellings is constructed in
reinforced concrete with timber window frames on the main
elevation. A second Tower Block, 240 ft. high and 122 ft. long
10 ft. is annexed to both blocks to accommodate
Lifts, staircase and other ancillary services.

The Eight-Storey Blocks (Nos. 1-4) rise to a
Height of cons. 80 ft. with brick case well
with timber window frames and reinforced concrete floor slabs.

The remaining Blocks (Nos. 17-19) are four Storey Blocks
and containing 24 dwellings. These are also erected in brick
with management yard buildings, hard landscaping, boiler
House, timber window frames and rough-finished pavement floors.

Pearsons with each common work on site and
Completion date is scheduled for early 1960.

Goodlass Wall & Company Limited of
Liverpool, founded in 1840, are one of the largest
paint manufacturers in the U.K. They are
wholly owned by the group - Goodlass Wall & Lead
Industries Limited. Whose other subsidiaries cover
a wide field in the refining of lead, antimony and
other non-ferrous metals, the manufacture of alloys,
stabilisers, smelting and other activities.
There are subsidiary paint and metal companies in
a number of overseas countries.

Originally concerned primarily with
decorative paints, Goodlass Wall subsequently built
up a dominant position in this field and are
also prominent in the Marine, Transport and Industrial
paint market. Their most recent development has
been the establishment of a separate Automotive
Section in their general industrial business and
it is in this field that the new equipment is,
initially, most relevant.

Devoe & Raynolds, a subsidiary of
the Celanese Corporation of America, is one of
the United States' oldest producers of
consumer paints, industrial finishes and a wide
range of chemicals, resins and plastics for coating
manufacturers and other industries. Founded in
1754 the Company is known as "The First American
Paint Maker" and today operates ten plants across
the United States.

Of Devoe's ten plants, two are at
Louisville, Ky., two are at Detroit, Michigan,
and one each is at Los Angeles and Riverside,
California; Houston, Texas; Princeton, Indiana;
Newark, New Jersey and Malden, Massachusetts.
The Company's executive offices and central
research facilities are located at Louisville.

C. H. STOKES (PRESS OFFICER)
1st January 1968.

1983-5236/46793

With great piles of earth building up in front of their
blades, the two machines moved forward, their tracks biting to
get a grip upon the slippery surface. Slowly the big tractor
forged ahead and finished a clear-cut ledge at its first
movement. To show how quickly such an operation can be done
in one day, and this gives a clear idea of the productivity
of the new British Caterpillar.

Later the two machines shed their bulldozers and were each
coupled to a big wheeled trailer called a scraper which works as
giant 'earth planes' and can pick up a load of up to 25 tons of
earth at a speed of up to 20 m.p.h. At this point the
depth at which earth is required. Again the new Caterpillar
showed its superior performance, picking up a load of nearly 25 tons of earth
and in less than a minute climbing a steep gradient and
dumping the earth in the distance clear out of sight.

So ended an impressive inauguration of great capacity
engineered to serve man's needs, for builders play so far an
increasing part in the daily life. To all who see them
produced. At one of the enormous building sites --
near and far where iron and steel plants would be erected, and coal and
iron ore to feed them, for examples. The British Caterpillar,
generously helped by American experts, has provided a new
beating heart in the new Caterpillar D8 tractor. A machine
which will also make a very valuable contribution to Britain's
export trade.

Undoubtedly, the proudest person who watched the demonstration
must have been the American Director of Manufacturing, who helped
to make possible the production of the British Caterpillar D8
and saw the first birth take place in his native land. For
Mr. J. R. Munro who directed the whole operation from building the
Caterpillar Birtley Factory to seeing the first British Caterpillar
D8 tractor roll off the assembly line in the heart of a four year
project is victory. Sir John J. H. Brown, who had arrived in the
United States on a boat, and is now Vice-President of the company.
As another Caterpillar official put it, "he has worked forty years
for this and it has been at the head of his mind that British
built Caterpillar D8 tractors out of the factory right on
schedule."

Dear Dr. Lamb:

Thank you very much for your letter of July 15, 1974 and for the
reprint of your article on trachoma. I am most interested in
your findings and will be happy to share them with our staff
members who are working on this problem.

We would also like to receive any further information you may
have on this subject as it becomes available.

Again, thank you for your thoughtfulness in sending us this material.

Sincerely yours,

John H. Costello

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Miscellaneous ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Accidents, Explosions, etc.
Transcribed_Text:
1983-5236/57895

Hold up damage Plse

Foreman told her ‘2 missing one dead’

“Herald” Reporter

A WORKS foreman walked past a Government security officer, out of the gates of a hush-hush factory in Stratford, E., late last night and approached an elderly man and two women standing on the kerb.

“Are you Mrs. Holmes?” he asked one of the women.

“Yes. Have you any news?” she replied.

He had. Two men were missing and one man was dead. They couldn’t be sure which was which, but among them was—Mr. Holmes.

His first day

As the foreman walked on, the group—father, wife and sister of Mr. Holmes—settled down to wait, all night if necessary, in an agony of uncertainty.

Three hours earlier, at 7.30, an explosion had wrecked a two-storey chemical distillery at the works of Boake Roberts, in Carpenter-row, E.

Mr. R. Wells, one of the directors, told me: “It was Holmes’ first day there. Normally only two men work in that building, but today Holmes was drafted in.

“It is a building used on fine chemical work. We are on secret work, and are under orders from the Board of Trade not to disclose anything.

“Our works fire brigade, under our NFS company officer, located one man, but the building was a sea of flame, and they could not get to him. He was brought out later.

“The whole building collapsed. We cannot tell whether the remaining two men, whom we fear are dead, are beneath the debris.”

Like blitz

It was like a blitz night in the East End.

A mobile NFS centre and radio station were set up to keep touch with NFS headquarters.

The other two men missing or dead are Sid Rounds, of Manor Park, E., and Jim Bushby, of West Ham.

All night a procession of relatives of the 15 men working in the factory called at the gate for news. But those injured only had slight cuts.

He's just up from the country, too

ALTHOUGH he's an aristocrat born and bred, Hoveton Marquis Barrington is a country boy at heart.

Quite worried he was, with all the palaver they made about this going up to London business. But, as you can see from the picture, everything is all right, now he's got to know Jackie Byatt.

Why, she even calls him George, just like they do down on the farm.

And George has got a message for his brother bullocks at Wroxham, Norfolk. These Londoners are middlin' fair folk, he says. . . .

Not stand-offish either, as you can see. Real friendly, our Jackie.

A 16-year-old Fulham school-girl, Jackie met George at Earls Court, where the Smithfield Show opens today. Now she's helping Mr. T. R. C. Blofeld's herdsman to get him ready for the judges.

Said Jackie: "I love animals—especially horses."

George let out a jealous bellow, so Jackie added: "And George best of all, of course."

Then she went to have a look at some of the other entries among the 1,500 cattle, sheep and pigs in the show.

title: A photographic print of Fishing, Fishermen - Miscellaneous
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Fishing ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Fishermen - Miscellaneous.
Transcribed_Text:
1983-5236/47701

By ALAN ROGERS
IN the shadow of an atom-age power-station, a fisherman crosses a mile of mud by a method the Romans used.
It is a striking illustration of man's high degree of civili- sation—and his backwardness.
In the background of the picture, taken at Hinkley Point in Somerset, is Britain's newest power-station.
It can produce enough elec- tricity to supply a city of nearly a million people.
In the foreground Brendan Sellick, aged 30, takes home his catch of shrimps on a mud-horse.
Mud-horses have been used on the shores of the Bristol Channel for nearly 2,000 years
to get across the desolate mud-flats, which are 8ft. deep in places.
The mud-horse is a wooden contraption like an upturned ironing board on which the fisherman puts his weight and pushes forward from the rear with his feet.
Said Mr. Sellick: "If we could find a better way to get out to our nets we could treble our catch. We are severely limited by the amount we can carry with us."
And despite the tricks of modern photography, there was only one way for SUN cameraman Dennis Webster to get this picture—by going out on a mud-horse. Just like the Romans would have done if they had had cameras.

WEBSTER.SUN.23.11.65.
Fishermen using the method of Transport used by the Romans near Hinkley Point (Somerset) Atom-Power station.

high hopes that the North Sea will yield vast quantities of gas to power

Ind - Misc - Trademarks etc.

Burmah
Garage sign in red, white and blue

Hard sell and mood of hope

BURMAH OIL'S clean-cut new symbol, which will gradually replace the Lobitos and Curfew names at the group's garages, reflects a feeling of "get-up-and-go."
Under the guidance of assistant managing director Nicholas Williams, aged 42, Burmah have embarked on an aggressive programme of expansion in the retail market.
The aim, he explained yesterday, is to push up the company's income in Britain from trading as opposed to investments. The first move was the take-over of the Castrol oil firm two years ago.
This was followed last month by the acquisition of the privately owned Curfew Petroleum cut-price chain, whose 135 petrol stations in the South and East fit in nicely with the 365-strong Lobitos chain, which are mainly in the North-West and Ireland.
Mr. Williams, who acquired much of his oil business know-how in India, says Burmah will be using hard-selling techniques to secure a market for the increased output of their refinery at Ellesmere Port, Cheshire.

OIL MEN DRILL ON THE ISLE OF WIGHT
November 30th 1952 PAR 32605-4 (Wo-R)

OIL MEN DRILL ON THE ISLE OF WIGHT........................

A derrick 136ft. high now towers over
the rural landscape at Perreton Farm,
Arreton - almost in the centre of
the Isle of Wight, summer holiday isle.
The D'Arcy Exploration Company,
prospecting subsidiary of the Anglo-
Iranian Oil Company, has begun
drilling for oil there.
The project may lead to a valuable
increase in petroleum from United
Kingdom soil, which already amounts
to 50,000 tons a year.
The drilling started last month, and
the bit has already reached a depth
of about 1,700ft.  The well will be
drilled to 8,000ft. if necessary.
Drilling on the Isle of Wight has
been planned for a number of years,
but no satisfactory location was
discovered until geophysical work
was undertaken.
The derrick in use at Arreton was
recently employed in exploration work
at Formby, Lancashire, where Anglo-
Iranian already operates a small
oilfield.
PICTURE SHOWS:-  A new length being
connected to the Arreton drill,
probing ever deeper into the earth.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION FRIDAY'S EVENINGS, May 16th.
TWO-STOREY STEEL HOUSES HELP THE SHORTAGE
16.5.47.
One of the very many different types of houses being erected
in various parts of the country in an effort to relieve the
great housing shortage, is a two-storey all-steel house.
These illustrated, in course of erection at HAYES, Middlesex,
have a steel cladding top storey, with mesh and cement-
rendered bottom walls. Some of the roofs are of aluminium,
others are of asbestos. The internal walls consist of light
wooden frames insulated with fibre glass mattress and finished
off with plaster board. The kitchens are furnished with all-
steel furniture, and the rooms are centrally heated from the
living room. Although they may not be quite so desirable to
some people as the good old brick-built residence, they are
fairly quick in erecting, and of course, are practically all
factory-built.

THEY WANT TO KEEP THE 'S' OUT OF STATE.....
London: Shareholders of Tate and Lyle, the sugar refiners, turned up in force for the extraordinary meeting held at the Caxton Hall, Westminster, (London), when the board sought the advice of the shreholders on what should be done to fight the threatened nationalization of the industry.
Sugar packets have already been issued by Tate and Lyle printed with anti-nationalization slogans, such as 'Keep the 'S' out of State', and "Untouched by Hand - Hands off Sugar!" Lord Lyle, the president of the company, and a former conservative Member of Parliament for Bournemouth, moved the resolution expressing the Board's views.

FOR WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS 2.10.46.

SEAPLANES WILL SEEK WHALES FOR FLOATING FACTORY

The United Whalers' 15000 ton factory ship BALAENA, first of its kind to be fitted with aircraft for whale-spotting, and weather reconnaissance, has been handed over to her owners after trials in Belfast Lough, and will shortly leave for the Antarctic in search of badly-needed whale-oil.
The ship will carry three converted Walrus amphibian aircraft, which will be launched from a double-action catapult working on a cordite charge, or lowered over the side for a normal water take-off by the crane which also lifts them from the water after a flight.
The Balaena will act as mother ship for a fleet of about ten whale-catchers, and her factory contains one of the largest oil-producing plants ever installed in a ship, and elaborate machinery for dealing with by-products: refrigerating plant will freeze the choicest parts of the whale meat for human consumption. The picture shows:
The BALAENA, showing the aperture in the stern through which the whales are hauled on board; above it is the flight deck on which one of the Walrus amphibians can be seen, and the crane.

THE QUEEN'S SPEECH ON THE OPENING OF PARLIAMENT

TUESDAY, 3RD NOVEMBER, 1964

MY LORDS AND MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

My Husband and I look forward with pleasure to our forthcoming visits to Ethiopia and the Sudan and to the Federal Republic of Germany. We were glad to be in Canada last month to attend the centennial celebrations commemorating the conferences held at Charlottetown and Quebec City in 1864 and to pay a further visit to Ottawa.

In international affairs it will be the principal purpose of My Ministers to seek to reduce East-West tension. To this end they will give renewed and more vigorous support to the United Nations in its vital role of freeing the world from the threat of war; and they will consider how this country can make a more effective contribution to the Organisation’s peace-keeping capability. They will seek to encourage further progress towards disarmament and to contribute to other steps which will permit the East-West conflict to be replaced by international co-operation in promoting peace and security throughout the world.

My Government reaffirm their support for the defence of the free world—the basic concept of the Atlantic Alliance; and they will continue to play their full part in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and in other organisations for collective defence. They will review defence policy to ensure, by relating our commitments and our resources, that My Armed Forces are able to discharge their many tasks overseas with the greatest effectiveness and economy. In particular, they will make constructive proposals for renewing the interdependence of the Atlantic Alliance in relation to nuclear weapons, in an endeavour to prevent duplication of effort and the dissemination of weapons of mass destruction.

New arrangements have been made to aid and encourage the economic and social advance of the developing nations, including the remaining dependent territories. My Ministers will also endeavour to promote the expansion of trade to this end, and they will seek, in co-operation with other countries and the United Nations and its agencies, to stimulate fresh action to reduce the growing disparities of wealth and opportunity between the peoples of the world.

My Ministers will have a special regard to the unique role of the Commonwealth, which itself reflects so many of the challenges and opportunities of the world. They will foster the Commonwealth connection on a basis of racial equality and close consultation between Member Governments and will promote Commonwealth collaboration in trade, economic development, educational, scientific and cultural contacts and in other ways.

My Government will continue to play a full part in the European organisations of which this country is a member and will seek to promote closer European co-operation.

A Bill will be introduced to provide for the independence of the Gambia.

2

MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

Estimates for the public services will be laid before you.

MY LORDS AND MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

At home My Government’s first concern will be to maintain the strength of sterling by dealing with the short-term balance of payments difficulties and by initiating the longer-term structural changes in our economy which will ensure purposeful expansion, rising exports and a healthy balance of payments.

Our industries will be helped to gain the full benefits of advances in scientific research and applied technology.

Central and regional plans to promote economic development, with special reference to the needs of the under-employed areas of the country, are being prepared. New arrangements will ensure proper attention to the needs of Wales. Legislation will be introduced to provide for the appointment of a Highland Development Board.

My Government will initiate early action to re-establish the necessary public ownership and control of the iron and steel industry.

To foster the health and prosperity of agriculture, they will continue the system of guarantees under the existing Acts and will promote measures to secure better marketing arrangements for farm produce. They will encourage the development of the fishing industry and the steady expansion of forestry.

My Government will call on trade unions and employers’ organisations to co-operate in eliminating those restrictive practices, on both sides of industry, which impair our competitive power and the development of the full potential of the economy. They will take steps to improve industrial efficiency by dealing more effectively with monopolies and with problems arising from mergers. They will also take action to improve the arrangements for industrial training and for the retraining of workers changing their employment. A Bill will be introduced to give workers and their representatives the protection necessary for freedom of industrial negotiation.

To the end that all may share the benefits of rising productivity, My Ministers will work for more stable prices and a closer relationship between the increase in productivity and the growth of incomes in all their forms; and they will promote reforms in taxation and better arrangements for local government finance. They will pay special attention to protecting the interests of consumers.

Action will be taken to require companies to disclose political contributions in their accounts.

My Government will have particular regard for those on whom age, sickness and personal misfortune impose special disabilities. They believe that radical changes in the national schemes of social security are essential to bring them into line with modern needs. They will therefore embark at once upon a major review of these schemes. Meanwhile, they will immediately introduce legislation to increase existing rates of National Insurance and associated benefits.

Now men, with doffed caps, are walking through the tiny villages of this Valley of Sorrow, breaking the news.
And at each house, as they leave, the curtains are drawn.

Among the victims are William Partridge, aged 40, and his son Tony, 20, and Roy Morgan and his 22-year-old son Colin.
Colin married a year ago. His 21-year-old wife Valerie sat at her hillside home, which overlooks the pit waiting, hoping. In her arms was her two-month-old son Jeffery.
Before the final news came she said: "Colin and his father began working in this part of the pit only yesterday."
A few minutes later she fainted.
The explosion ripped through the west district of Arrael Griffin Colliery at 11.45 a.m. Seven hundred men were below ground at the time.
As those away from the blast area were brought to the surface, rescue workers with breathing masks hurried below.
They carried canaries, still the surest method of testing for the deadly pit gas. And hopes for the men faded as all the canaries died as soon as the men reached the pit bottom.
A huge fall of rock blocked the roadway. Relays of men tore at it, as others tried to shore up the weakened roof.
Then, as the sun was sinking behind the hillside 1,000 feet above them, they burst through.

COAL BOARD
DENT. AT
SEE DA FEAT.

LORD ROBENS, the Coal Board chairman, has 529,979 workers on his payroll drawing an average of £16 for a 40-hour week.
But his 529,980th employee is a dream. This worker does a stint of 70 hours a week for pay of £8. And what's more—with never a grumble.
Who is this best-ever bargain in the labour market? It is 66-year-old, homely Mrs. Rachael Dent. For 42 years she has worked as a char at Grimethorpe Colliery, Yorkshire, cleaning the offices.
It has never occurred to her that the hours are long. She just loves her work. And her pride won't let her skimp it to get the job done in a reasonable time.
A typical day in Mrs. Dent's life starts at 5.30 p.m. Mrs. Dent moves in and scrubs and polishes until the early hours of the morning. And she does this seven days a week.
At her house near the colliery Mrs. Dent told me: "I suppose some people think I am daft working these hours, but I enjoy work. It is my only real interest in life."
Then she sat down to map out her daily time-table of toil. She usually begins with the officials' bath house.
Next stop is the group manager's office. The entire place is dusted and swept and the floor polished. The same treatment is given to the clerks' office and the rest room, with its two bathrooms and toilet.

The big job
Then she moves on to the group accountant's office, the pensions office and more bathrooms.
After that she faces her really big job—the huge wages office.
In addition to all this she does her own housework, and looks after her husband and their invalid son.
What does the Coal Board think of this champion char?
An official spokesman in Doncaster said:
"Mrs. Dent officially works an eight-hour day and is paid according to the appropriate scale laid down.
"What extra work she might do in her own time is her own affair."
The Coal Board can't shrug her off as haughtily as that.
There is clearly more work than can be done properly in the official 40 hours.
I suggest one of those Coal Board chappies takes over Mrs. Dent's job for a week—and then you bet something would be done!
David Farr

MAKING THE CORONATION CARPET ON THE LARGEST
LOOMS IN SCOTLAND. 10.3.37.

The carpet that is to be laid in Westminster Abbey for
the Coronation ceremony is now being carefully made in a Glas-
gow Mill. The carpet has several special features. It is one
of the biggest ever made, the pieces, of which there are many,
are 40ft. x 35ft. and the surface is getting special treatment
to make it as smooth as glass, this has been found necessary to
allow the flowing trains of the royal ladies and peeresses who
will walk on it, an easy passage,as any minute obstruction would
catch in the frail material they will wear. The carpet, owing
to its gigantic size, is being made on the largest looms in
Scotland, of Messrs. TEMPLETON of Glasgow, who also made the
Coronation carpet for King George V when he was crowned in 1912.
The Scots girls who are now working on the carpet feel delighted
to be sharing in the work for this historic ceremony and are
taking extra special care at all stages of progress to produce the
finest example of carpet making.

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Agriculture ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â» Vegetables - Cabbage, Broccoli, etc.
Transcribed_Text:
1983-5236/41729

THE cauliflower I am holding in the picture above measures 3¾ inches by 4¾ inches, weighs 13 ounces including stalk, and when cooked would provide barely enough for two people.
It was sold retail for 10d., and housewives complained—with justification—that it was too dear.
But a few hours earlier it had been bought by the greengrocer wholesale for 1s. 1d.
Such are the strange economics of the vegetable market at the moment.
The cauliflower was one of six dozen bought by a retailer. For each crate of two dozen he paid 26s., averaging 1s. 1d. each wholesale.

Market price
Why did he pay that price? Because that was the market price and the cauliflowers on the top of the crates seemed a decent size.
On opening them he found that more than half were very small.
He sold four at 6d., eight at 10d., 28 at 1s. 1d., and 32 at 1s. 6d., making a gross profit of 9s. on an outlay of £3 18s.
Everybody was unhappy—
The GREENGROCER, because he wasn’t making much money; his CUSTOMERS, because prices were high;
the GROWER, because rain had spoilt much of his crop.
Even the WHOLESALER was unhappy. Although assured of his commission he would like to sell twice as many.
Why is this happening? There are two main reasons:
1 Incessant rain has reduced supplies and prices are being forced up.
2 Bad packing and marketing give the retailer no guarantee that when he buys 24 vegetables in a box they will all be the same size or quality.

RESTORATION WORK AT ETON COLLEGE. EH/MEG

Extensive restoration work is now in progress on the Cloisters
of Eton College, the cost of which is being borne by the Eton
Antkafa Appeal Fund, to which the Dulverton Trustees have
contributed the sum of £20,000 to be expended on this work,
Restoration has been made necessary due to the following defects
(a)general deterioration of stonework; (b) flaking of the stone
facing on the upper part of the Cloisters; (c) dry rot and
death watch beetle in roof timbers; (d) on the upper part of the
Cloisters, the bonding between the outer stone facing and the
brick wall behind it, was no longer effective, resulting in
bulging of the outer stone wall which had become dangerous in
places. The original stone used on the Cloisters, believed to
be in some form of Clunch, is being replaced by Clipsham Stone
from Rutland, which is much more hard-wearing.

Photograph shows :- Stone-mason JAMES WINCH, of Ascot, using
his mallet and chisel with expert skill as he works on the
restoration of one of the Arches in the Cloisters of Eton College.

"GRAVEYARD OF GIANTS"
WHERE BATTLESHIPS GO FOR SCRAP  DG/PR

"Abandon Hope All Ye That Enter Here" is the ironic
warning over the entrance to the jetty of Messrs.
Thomas Ward, shipbreakers, of Inverkeithing ,
Scotland, and so far as warships are concerned, the
phrase applies down to the last rivet.
Wards are the biggest shipbreakers in Britain, and
one of the largest in the world.  Not only are they
the biggest shipbreakers, but they break up the
biggest ships.   To their yards-and to others
such as Metal Industries, or Arnott and Young's-
come such floating giants as "Rodney", Revenge",
"Renown"; the "New York", once Hitler's "strength
through joy" liner, and many others.  Mighty fighting
ships which sailed triumphantly through two world
wars, find their last resting place under scrapyard
cranes.   Guns which the combined fleets of
the Third Reich and Imperial Japanese Navy, failed
to muzzle, are silent, as hissing oxy-acetylene
cutters carve into their vitals.
Much of the valuable scrap goes to sea again in
the form of new ships, and thus fights in Britain's
export drive.  Brass, copper and much needed alloys
are sent to Sheffield, while metal scrap goes to
Newcastle.

" Herald " Reporter
HERE is the cameraman's view of the closing stage of the Battle of the Second Floor Back, which ended yesterday at Houghton-place, N.W., in victory for the tenant.
The battle began six weeks ago when Mr. Charles O'Leary was evicted from his single room by Mrs. Eliades after a Tribunal had reduced his rent from £2 10s. to 17s. 6d.
Three days ago St. Pancras Borough Council requisitioned the room—but a new lock on the street door kept Mr. O'Leary and his wife out.
So the Town Clerk, acting under the powers recently given by Mr. Bevan, requisitioned the whole house.
When Mr. O'Leary and council officials went along yesterday to take possession they found the front door open—but there was a new lock on the door of his flat.
" Break it open, " said the Housing Manager to the council's joiner—and here you see him doing it, with Mr. O'Leary looking on.
Within a few minutes the lock had been replaced by another and two keys given to Mr. O'Leary.

JON-

FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS AUGUST 11th.
POST-WAR PLANNING IN WARTIME -
A NEW £1,000,000 TOWN FOR WAR WORKERS.
Mr Ernest Brown, Minister of Health, recently performed
the opening ceremony of a self-contained community of
844 new houses for war workers transferred from London
for a new industry in the Midlands, which will remain
after the war. The scheme, which has been completed by
the rural district council at a cost of £1,000,000, gives
each house an eighth of an acre of garden, electric
light and power, running water and main drainage; at a
maximum weekly rent of 17/9d, inclusive ofrates; nearly
700 workers already occupy these model houses, whose
construction, practically eliminating the use of wood,
solves a major problem of post-war building. 15 acres
of ground have been reserved for new junior and senior
schools, and there will be three churches and a cinema.
There is already a fine shopping centre, complete with
Post Office. The pictures show:-
1. A type of 3-bedroom-and-parlour house, let at
15/6d. per week inclusive of rates.
2. The living-room of a 3-bedroom and parlour DUPLICATE SENT MANCHESTER
type house, let at 13/7d. per week inclusive
of rates. The combination grate heats water 11-8-43
for household purposes, the floor is concrete,
and steel-framed french windows lead to an
eighth of an acre of garden.
